## The future of hiring without resumes, what comes next?
URL: https://learn.zero.university/learn/the-future-of-hiring-without-resumes
Home / Learn / The future of hiring without resumes, what comes next? CORNERSTONE The future of hiring without resumes, what comes next? The resume is already dead for the companies that actually read the data, and what replaces it is not a shinier PDF or a video pitch but direct proof of skill: scored, verifiable work evaluated against a professional bar, shifting hiring from filtering on pedigree to matching on evidence. Resume use fell to 67% of employers in 2025, down from 73% the year before, a rapid collapse as skills-based practices take over ( TestGorilla State of Skills-Based Hiring 2025 ). 85% of employers now use skills-based hiring, up from 81% in 2024 ( TestGorilla 2025 ). Only 31% of employers who dropped degree requirements actually followed through with real change, with fewer than 1 in 700 hires reflecting that shift ( Burning Glass Institute + HBS ). New-grad hiring at big tech is down more than 50% from 2019, and new grads now make up roughly 7% of hires ( SignalFire State of Talent Report 2025 ). Why did the resume stop working? The resume was never a measure of ability but a sorting mechanism for a world where employers could not see the work: you listed credentials, companies scanned for brand names and keywords, and the actual capacity to do the job was inferred from where you went to school or who previously employed you. That inference is collapsing under the weight of its own inaccuracy. When 85% of employers adopt skills-based hiring, the market is explicitly admitting that the document filtering them for decades is a poor proxy for output. Resumes compress a human into bullet points that anyone can write and few can verify, rewarding formatting and keyword stuffing rather than execution. The decline is not a prediction, it is a measured trend: resume use dropped six percentage points in a single year. Companies are not waiting for a better PDF, they are routing around the document entirely. If not resumes, then what replaces them? The replacement is not a single new document type but a structural shift toward proof. Employers want to see what you can build, decide, and ship before they make an offer, which takes the form of scored simulations, project-based assessments, and verifiable work product evaluated against a professional standard. This is the Google ads algorithm for people: instead of bidding on keywords, you are matched on demonstrated capability. The old path of collecting credentials and hoping someone notices is being replaced by building proof and getting matched directly to the work that actually wants you. Platforms that host real scenarios for real companies, score the output against the top 1% of professionals, and put that evidence in front of recruiters are the structural replacement, a shift from claiming skill on paper to proving it in practice. Why are skills-based hiring pledges stalling? The raw adoption numbers look like a revolution: 53% of employers dropped degree requirements, a 77% increase year over year. But the follow-through tells a different story, because fewer than 1 in 700 hires at companies that announced these drops actually saw a change in who got the job. The degree reset is largely a public relations move, not a structural one. The gap exists because companies removed the credential filter but failed to install a proof mechanism in its place. Without a scored, verifiable signal of ability, recruiters default right back to the brand names they know. Dropping a requirement is easy, but replacing it with a better signal requires new infrastructure, which means installing evaluated work product as the trustworthy evidence rather than just hoping the old filter is not needed. What does a proof-based hiring loop look like in practice? In a proof-based loop, the candidate does not apply with a biography but engages with a real scenario, submits their work, and receives specific feedback on what they did well and what needs fixing, while the recruiter sees scored output rather than self-reported claims. Students in early pilots were not interested in generic skill assessments or hand-holding tutorials: they wanted to do real work within 90 seconds of logging in, and they returned to the platform specifically to see feedback on their submissions. Per-submission feedback drove every return visit, while generic advice was ignored. When the heavy onboarding scaffolding was removed and replaced with a single task pickup screen, activation increased substantially. The loop that works is attempt, get evaluated, iterate, get matched. How does zero fit into the post-resume market? zero is built for the structural replacement, not the patch. Students work through company-shaped scenarios, their output is scored against the top 1% of professionals in that domain, and recruiters pay to access a pool of pre-vetted talent, a model that is free for students and recruiter-paid, which flips the incentive from filtering masses of applicants to matching proven ones. The pilot data confirms that the engagement hook is not the certificate at the end but the scored feedback on real work. Students said they would rather submit something rough and get real feedback than read another article about marketing, and that preference for iteration over consumption is the foundation of a post-resume hiring system. You do not need to summarize your life on a page when your work is already evaluated and visible. What happens to recruiters and job boards? Recruiters and job boards currently exist to bridge the information gap between a candidate's claims and an employer's verification, and when the work itself is the application, that gap closes. Keyword-matching job boards stuffed with optimized resumes become obsolete, and recruiters who actually source talent become far more efficient when they can sort by scored proof instead of guessing from a LinkedIn profile. The big tech numbers make the economics clear: new grads are roughly 7% of hires at major tech companies, down over 50% from 2019. Companies are not hiring fewer people overall, they are shedding the entry-level filter that relied on campus prestige and resume keywords. The talent organizations that survive this shift will be the ones that consolidate verified talent and make it searchable by demonstrated capability, not by self-reported history. Frequently asked questions Will I still need a resume at all? Yes, for now, because legacy systems die slowly, but relying on one is betting on a dying format. The trend is clear: resume reliance is dropping, and the companies winning at early-career hiring are the ones evaluating work product directly. A resume is becoming a fallback, not the primary currency. How do I show proof of skill if I have no work experience? You build it. Simulations, project-based scenarios, and scored challenges let you generate professional-level evidence without needing a prior job. Employers care about what you can do, not where you learned to do it. Are skills-based hiring platforms free for candidates? zero is free for students. The cost is covered by recruiters who pay for access to a pre-vetted, scored talent pool, which aligns incentives: the platform succeeds when it produces real matches, not when it charges applicants for visibility. Why did companies announce degree drops but not follow through? They removed a filter without installing a replacement. Without a reliable proof mechanism, recruiters defaulted back to the signals they know, which are brand names and degrees. Dropping the requirement is the easy part, replacing it with scored evidence is the hard structural work. What makes a scored simulation different from a portfolio? Unlike a self-curated portfolio highlight reel, a scored simulation evaluates your work against a professional bar, provides specific feedback, and produces a verifiable metric that is objective evidence of capability. Most side projects die in the description because they read like hobbies, not decisions with consequences. Reframe them as scored proof of specific skills used in real roles, and recruiters will treat them as work experience. Resume use fell to 67% in 2025, down from 73% the year before, as employers hunt for proof beyond the page, TestGorilla State of Skills-Based Hiring 2025 53% of employers have dropped degree requirements, up 77% year-over-year, but fewer than 1 in 700 hires reflected real change, TestGorilla 2025 and Burning Glass Institute + HBS Internship-to-full-time conversion sits at 63.1%, the single most influential factor between equally qualified candidates, NACE The gap between "I built something" and "hire me" is not the project, it is the scoring layer that translates it into recruiter language why most side projects fail the recruiter test The project itself is rarely the problem. The framing is. Recruiters scan for three signals: scope, stakes, and skill match. Most side project descriptions hit none. "Built a personal finance app in React" tells a recruiter you have free time and a tutorial completion streak, not whether you made architectural decisions under constraint, whether anyone else used it, or whether you iterated after failure. The filter operating system of school trained you to list activities, but employers need decision records. A course teaches you syntax, while a shipped project with user complaints, a pivot, and a performance bottleneck you solved becomes a decision record with consequences, the translation layer most people skip. The honest reason side projects get dismissed: the person reading your resume has seen "passion project" code that never ran in production, never had a user, never required a tradeoff. They are not wrong to be skeptical. Your job is to make the skepticism impossible. the four elements that make self-directed work credible Recruiters who actually hire from side projects look for specific evidence. Build your description around these four: Constraint. What limited you? Time, money, a platform's API limits, a team member who quit? "Built in 72 hours for a hackathon deadline" or "Rewrote after first version crashed at 100 concurrent users" shows engineering under pressure, not leisure coding. Stake. Who besides you cared about the outcome? Real users, a client who paid, a community that complained? "Open-sourced and got 14 issues filed" beats "available on GitHub." Money is the clearest stake, but attention works too. If nobody noticed, say what you did to try to make them notice and why it failed. Honesty about failed distribution is still a decision record. Sequence. What did you do first, what did you abandon, and why? "Started with Firebase, hit scaling limits, migrated to PostgreSQL in week three" shows you can throw away sunk cost. The filter OS punishes failure. Professional work requires it. Skill match. Do not list every technology you touched. Match the job's stated requirements with specific project moments. If they want "cross-functional collaboration," describe the argument with your designer friend about navigation hierarchy. If they want "product sense," describe the feature you cut because usage data showed nobody clicked it. how to write the project so it reads like a job The structure that works is not "what I built" but "what problem I owned, what I tried, what happened." Bad: "Created a web scraper to track apartment prices." Good: "Noticed friends were manually checking 12 rental sites; built a scraper that reduced search time from 3 hours to 10 minutes; hit Craigslist's rate limit in week two, switched to cached polling architecture; 23 friends used it for 4 months, then I shut it down when a paid competitor launched and I analyzed why their UX won." The second version has scope (rental market, not "web scraper"), stakes (friends depended on it), sequence (rate limit → architecture change), and a real ending (shutdown, competitive analysis). That is a product manager's decision record, and it is also an engineer's: the same project, two different skill matches, depending on the role. Use numbers that mean something to the role. Engineers: latency, throughput, error rate reduction. Marketers: acquisition cost, conversion funnel, retention. Designers: task completion time, error rate in user tests, iterations after feedback. Generic "grew to 500 users" is weak unless you say how and at what cost. where to put it so recruiters actually see it The resume is not the only channel, and for scored work it is increasingly not the best one. Recruiters spend seconds on resumes because they are low-signal documents. A GitHub link in a resume line is a gesture, not evidence. The recruiter will not click it. The hiring manager might, if the resume already passed filters. The better path: put the proof where the recruiter already works. LinkedIn projects are barely better than resume lines. A short Loom walkthrough of the project, posted where the role's community actually gathers (Substack, Twitter/X, relevant Discord, industry Slack), builds ambient credibility. The ideal is a scored submission against a professional bar, something the recruiter can open and see ranked against other candidates, which functions like the Google ads algorithm for people: your work surfaces when the role matches, not when you beg for attention. If you must use the traditional resume, give the project its own section titled "Independent Work" or "Self-Directed Projects," not "Hobbies." Put it above unrelated internships. Order by relevance to the role, not chronology. when a side project is not enough (and what to add) Some gaps a project cannot close alone. Know them honestly. Collaboration is the hardest to fake solo. If the role requires "leading cross-functional teams," one project where you argued with a friend is thin. Supplement with open-source contribution where you navigated maintainers' feedback, or explicit documentation of how you sought out users, handled complaints, or coordinated with a remote collaborator. Scale is the other gap. A project used by 20 people is real work, but it is not the same constraint as serving 20,000. Be honest about scale, then show what you did to prepare for it: load testing, architecture decisions made with growth in mind, the feature you deferred to keep performance stable. The final gap is external validation, where self-reported skill is noise and scored work against a standard the employer recognizes is signal. The old path collects credentials and hopes someone notices, while the new one builds proof and gets matched to the work that actually wants you. frequently asked questions How long does a side project need to run to count as experience? Duration matters less than density of decisions. A two-week sprint with real users, failure, and iteration beats six months of occasional tinkering with no stakes. Signal the intensity, not the calendar time. Can I count a project I built for a class or bootcamp? Only if you extended it beyond the assignment. "Built what the instructor specified" is coursework. "Used the class project as a base, then added a feature based on user feedback, deployed it, and got 50 signups" is self-directed work with a starting constraint. The extension is what counts. What if my project failed completely? Failure with documentation is stronger than success with none. Describe the hypothesis, the test, the result, and what you would do differently. Shutdown analysis is standard professional practice. Most candidates hide failure. You will stand out by owning it with specificity. Should I list technologies or outcomes? Outcomes first, technologies only as evidence for the outcome. "React, Node, MongoDB" is a stack. "Reduced load time from 4.2s to 800ms by switching from MongoDB aggregations to cached Redis queries" is a decision record that happens to name technologies. How do I handle a project where I was the only user? Be honest and add distribution attempts. "Built for personal use, then posted on Reddit and got 12 downloads, 3 angry emails about crashes, fixed the top bug" is stronger than pretending you had users. The attempt and response to feedback is the work experience. ## Can I Use Club Leadership as Work Experience on My Resume?
URL: https://learn.zero.university/learn/use-club-leadership-as-work-experience-resume
Home / Learn / Can I Use Club Leadership as Work Experience on My Resume? CORNERSTONE Can I Use Club Leadership as Work Experience on My Resume? Yes, if you translate it into business outcomes. Recruiters do not care that you were "president." They care that you managed a $4,000 budget, grew membership 40%, or ran an event for 200 people. The mistake is listing the title. The move is listing the proof. 53% of employers have dropped degree requirements, up from 30% the year before, which means they are actively hunting for signals of skill outside formal work history, TestGorilla State of Skills-Based Hiring 2025 Resume use fell to 67% as employers shift toward work samples and skills verification, same TestGorilla report An internship cuts underemployment odds by 48.5%, but structured extracurricular leadership with measurable outputs is the closest substitute when you have no internship, Strada Institute + Burning Glass Institute, "Talent Disrupted" The framing gap: most students list responsibilities, while recruiters search for impact metrics in the same line Why most club leadership gets ignored Recruiters spend six to ten seconds on a first scan. They are not reading, they are pattern-matching for evidence of capability. "President, Finance Club" is a label, not evidence. It joins three hundred other "presidents" in the pile and signals nothing distinct. The filter is not snobbery about paid versus unpaid work. It is the lack of translation. You ran a club in a context where nothing was at stake, no revenue changed hands, and no one got fired for failure. The recruiter cannot tell if you showed up to meetings or built something real. Their default assumption, given no data, is the former. This is the same problem degrees face in the shift to skills-based hiring, where the title is a proxy that used to carry weight. As 53% of employers drop degree requirements , they are also dropping their patience for proxy signals that do not resolve into proof. Club leadership sits in the same bucket: valuable if substantiated, noise if bare. How to turn a club role into resume ammunition The formula is verb, scale, outcome. Not "organized events." "Recruited 12 corporate sponsors, raised $8,500, and ran a 200-person career fair that placed 34 students in interviews." The second version contains six distinct professional competencies: business development, financial management, logistics, marketing, partnership negotiation, and outcome tracking. Apply this to every bullet. If you were treasurer, do not write "managed club finances." Write "built a zero-based budget for 60 members, collected $12,000 in dues, and reduced year-end waste 22% by switching vendors." If you were social chair, do not write "planned events." Write "grew attendance from 35 to 140 across four events by A/B testing invitation channels; 67% of attendees joined the mailing list." The test is whether a stranger could hire you for a paid role based on that line alone. If the bullet describes a task any member could claim, rewrite it until it describes a result only you delivered. Where to place it on your resume There are two valid moves, depending on what else you have. If you have zero internships, part-time jobs, or freelance work, club leadership belongs in a section called "Leadership & Projects" or "Selected Experience," not buried under "Activities." The goal is proximity to eye-tracking heat. Recruiters scan top-third first. Burying your strongest evidence at the bottom is self-sabotage. If you have some work experience, club leadership can live in a separate "Leadership" section below your paid roles. The hierarchy signals that you know the difference between revenue-generating work and mission-driven work, while still claiming the transferable skills. Never put it under "Education" as a sub-bullet. That section is for coursework, GPA, and honors. Mixing operational achievements with academic credentials confuses the scan and wastes the space where you could have put another impact line. What recruiters actually cross-check The drop in resume reliance to 67% reflects a broader shift. Employers are adding work samples, skills assessments, and structured interviews to their process. This means your club bullet is not the finish line. It is the hook that gets you into a stage where you must demonstrate the skill. Prepare for that stage. If you wrote "negotiated $5,000 in sponsorships," be ready to explain your outreach sequence, your rejection rate, your pitch revision, and the specific terms you secured. If you wrote "grew membership 40%," know your baseline, your channels, your cost per acquisition, and why the growth rate flattened or accelerated. The resume gets the interview. The story behind the bullet gets the offer. This is where most candidates leak credibility. They optimize the document and neglect the narrative. A number without backup becomes a liability the moment a recruiter probes. The honest limit of club leadership There is a ceiling. Running a club is not running a P&L. Managing a $3,000 budget is not managing $300,000. Recruiters at senior hiring levels know the difference and will discount accordingly. The move is not to pretend equivalence. It is to extract the maximum transferable proof from the actual scale you operated at, then close the gap with other evidence as you build it. An internship cuts underemployment odds by 48.5% because it provides supervised, consequential work in a real organizational context. Club leadership is the best available substitute, not an equivalent replacement. Use it aggressively while you have it. Replace it as soon as you can with scored work that a recruiter can evaluate directly. That last point is the structural shift. The old path was: club leadership → internship → full-time role, each stage validating the next. The new path, as skills-based hiring expands , is: any proof of skill → direct evaluation → role match. Club leadership can enter that pipeline if the proof is real and the metrics are specific. The certificate you got for attending six meetings cannot. Frequently asked questions Should I list every club, or just the leadership roles? Just the leadership roles with measurable output. Membership without responsibility signals participation, not capability. One strong leadership entry beats four passive memberships. What if my club was small or informal? Scale honestly but emphasize the constraint. "Built a 15-person tutoring network with no budget, matching 40 students to volunteers in three weeks" shows resourcefulness that a 200-person club with funding cannot claim. Do I need to prove the numbers I list? Keep them truthful and defensible. Recruiters rarely audit, but the question "how did you measure that" comes up in interviews. If you estimated, say "estimated based on sign-in sheets." Precision without integrity collapses faster than rough honesty. How does this compare to a portfolio project? A portfolio project with visible code, design, or writing is stronger evidence because it is inspectable. Club leadership wins on collaboration, stakeholder management, and execution under ambiguity. Lead with the project if you have it, add the club role to show you can ship with other humans involved. When should I remove club leadership from my resume? After two to three years of full-time work, or once you have two stronger professional entries that cover the same competencies. It ages out faster than paid experience because the stakes were lower, even if the skills were real. ## can i use ai to do my portfolio project and still claim it as my work?
URL: https://learn.zero.university/learn/using-ai-for-portfolio-project-claim-as-your-work
Home / Learn / can i use ai to do my portfolio project and still claim it as my work? CORNERSTONE can i use ai to do my portfolio project and still claim it as my work? Claiming AI-generated work as your own collapses the second someone asks why you built it that way. The line is decision ownership: if you directed the choices and can defend them under pressure, the work is yours regardless of what tool executed it. 85% of employers now use skills-based hiring practices that test your actual ability, not your self-reported toolchain ( TestGorilla 2025 ) Resume reliance dropped to 67% as employers shift to proof-of-skill verification over paper claims ( TestGorilla 2025 ) Employers are scrutinizing the work itself far more closely as they move beyond paper credentials The line is decision ownership: if you made the call and can explain it, the work is yours regardless of what tool executed it An internship cuts underemployment odds by 48.5% because employers verify you can actually do the job, not just describe it ( Strada + Burning Glass Institute ) what does "your work" actually mean when ai exists? Every professional tool does part of the job for you. Your compiler catches syntax errors, your linter flags bad patterns, your framework generates boilerplate. Nobody asks if you "really" wrote the code when your IDE auto-completes a function signature. The question was always about where the thinking happened. AI shifts the boundary because it can generate entire structures, not just fill gaps. But the principle is the same: the work belongs to whoever made the decisions. If you chose the problem, defined the constraints, evaluated the outputs, iterated on the failures, and can articulate why the final version exists as it does, you did the work. The AI was a very fast intern executing your instructions. Pasting a prompt, accepting the first response, and uploading it means the AI did the work and you were a courier. The distinction is not about which buttons you pressed, it is about who was driving. A senior engineer uses Copilot to ship faster, but she reviews every line, rejects the bad suggestions, and owns the architecture, which makes it her code. A junior who accepts every suggestion without reading it is not writing code but forwarding emails from a machine. how do recruiters test whether you built it or a machine did? They ask you to change it. Live. On a call, in an interview, or in a follow-up task, a hiring manager will say "walk me through this component" or "how would you modify this if the requirement changed to X?" If you built it, this is easy. You know the tradeoffs, the dead ends you tried first, the constraints that shaped the final shape. If the AI built it and you submitted it, you will stare at your own portfolio like it was written in a language you do not speak. This is why skills-based hiring is accelerating. When 85% of employers use skills-based practices, they are not checking your tools, they are checking your judgment. They want to see if you can reason about work, not just present it. A portfolio that survives a "why this way?" interrogation is proof, while one that crumbles under the same question is a liability. The old system let you hide behind credentials, where a degree from a name-brand school signaled "probably competent" without anyone checking the actual work. When 53% of employers dropped degree requirements , that signal got weaker. Now the work itself has to hold up. If you used AI to skip the learning, the work will not hold up, and the interview will expose the gap immediately. what is the honest way to use ai in a portfolio project? Use it the way professionals use calculators. You do the math in your head to estimate, then verify with the calculator. You do not hand in a calculator output and call it your solution. Concrete rules for the line: Use AI to scaffold, not to ship. Generate a first draft of a component, then rewrite it with your own logic. The AI gave you a starting point, not a finished product. Use AI to learn, not to skip. Ask it to explain a concept you do not understand, then apply that understanding yourself. If you cannot reproduce the reasoning without the AI, you did not learn it. Use AI to accelerate iteration, not to replace it. Get five variations of a headline, pick one, then edit it until it sounds like your voice. The selection and refinement are your work; the raw options are the machine's. Document your process. If you used AI, say so. "I used GPT to generate the initial data model, then refactored it for our access patterns" is a senior-level explanation. Hiding it is a junior-level mistake. The filter OS that runs traditional education trains you to hide your process and present only the polished output. That habit will hurt you here. Transparency about your workflow signals confidence and maturity, while secrecy invites recruiters to probe harder because it looks like you have something to hide. what happens if you get caught claiming ai work as your own? The same thing that happens when anyone claims credit for work they did not do: you lose trust, and trust is the only currency that matters in hiring. A recruiter who catches you inflating your contribution will not just reject you for that role, they will remember your name. The industry is smaller than you think. But the bigger cost is internal. When you submit AI-generated work as your own, you skip the struggle that builds the skill. The struggle is the point. Every professional you admire got good by being bad, getting feedback, and trying again. If you outsource the struggle to a language model, you keep the credential but lose the capability. Then you show up to a job where people expect you to perform, and you cannot, because the capability was never built. This is the degree-as-mortgage problem applied at the project level: you borrowed competence instead of money, and now you owe it back with interest. The difference is that a lender cannot repossess your knowledge, but an employer absolutely can repossess your job when they realize you cannot do the work. how should you present ai-assisted work in your portfolio? State it clearly and move on. "Built with AI assistance for boilerplate generation; all architecture decisions, business logic, and testing by me." That sentence tells a recruiter exactly what they need to know: you are efficient, you use modern tools, and you know where the machine ends and your judgment begins. Include process notes. Show the prompt you wrote, the raw output you got, and the edits you made. That sequence is more impressive than the final artifact, because it demonstrates taste, critical thinking, and iteration. Anyone can generate output. Editing raw generation into something good is a rare skill. If you built the project on zero, the platform's vision is to capture this naturally. You submit work, and the goal is to get scored against a professional bar, with a feedback loop designed to show what you changed and why. The vision is for the score to be proof of your capability, not your toolchain. Whether you used AI to help write the first draft or typed every character by hand, the aim is for the score to reflect what you can actually defend and deliver. Do not over-explain or apologize for using AI. Every engineer at every major company uses it now. The question is never "did you use AI?" The question is "can you do the work without it if you have to?" If the answer is yes, you have nothing to worry about. frequently asked questions is it cheating to use chatgpt for a portfolio project? No, as long as you directed the decisions and can defend the result. Using AI to generate, refine, or debug is standard professional practice. Submitting unedited AI output as your own work is misrepresentation, not tool use. should i disclose that i used ai in my portfolio? Yes. A brief note like "AI-assisted for boilerplate; all logic and decisions by me" shows maturity and transparency. Hiding it creates more risk than disclosing it. what if a recruiter asks me to rebuild something without ai? If you actually built the skill, you can rebuild it slower. If you cannot, you relied on the AI as a crutch, not a tool, and the interview will reveal that gap. can i use ai-generated code in a take-home assignment? Check the company's policy. If they allow it, disclose it. If they forbid it, follow the rule. Violating a stated policy is an automatic rejection, regardless of the code quality. does zero allow ai assistance on submissions? Yes. zero's vision is to score what you submit against a professional bar. Your toolchain is your problem. The aim is for the score to reflect whether the work meets the standard, not which tools you used to reach it. ## What do recruiters look at when a student has no work experience?
URL: https://learn.zero.university/learn/what-do-recruiters-look-at-when-a-student-has-no-work-experience
Learn / What recruiters look at THE NO-EXPERIENCE READ What do recruiters look at when a student has no work experience? Recruiters look at proxies: school name, GPA, whether your keywords matched the posting. None of those prove you can do the job, and most applications get only seconds before the verdict. The one thing that actually changes the read is scored proof of work, a real task in the role they can judge for themselves. No experience means no accomplishments to skim, so recruiters fall back on proxies (school, GPA, keywords) and most applications get only seconds. Those proxies are losing their grip: 85% of employers now use skills-based hiring, up from 81% , prioritizing demonstrated ability (TestGorilla, 2025). The strongest move a no-experience candidate has is a real, scored work sample in the target role, not a longer list of claims. Evidence wins because a recruiter can judge it directly and fast, instead of guessing from a resume. The stakes are not abstract: about 41.5% of recent graduates are underemployed , working jobs their degree never required (NY Fed). What actually happens when you apply with nothing to show Picture the recruiter's side for a second, because it is not flattering and nobody tells you this. They are staring at a giant pile of applications, software has already filtered some out, and the ones that survive get a few seconds of human attention each. For a candidate with a real work history, those seconds land on what they shipped and where. For a student with none, there is nothing to land on, so the eye slides to proxies: which school, what GPA, did the keywords match. That is not the recruiter being lazy. It is the only thing in the file to read. The trap is that none of those proxies answer the one question the job actually has, which is whether you can do the work. So strong students get filtered out before anyone forms a real opinion of them, and they walk away convinced they are the problem. You are not the problem. The file is empty of the only signal that counts, and you can fix that. Why a thicker resume does not fix it The instinct is to write more. Add another bullet, pad the projects section, list the coursework. It rarely works, because you are adding more claims to a document a recruiter already knows is a sales pitch. Everyone's resume says they are a fast learner, a team player, detail-oriented. The reader discounts all of it on sight, because a resume is a list of things you say about yourself, and no recruiter mistakes a claim for proof. This is also why the usual student toolkit only takes you so far. A Coursera or Udemy certificate, a LinkedIn Learning badge, a Forage simulation you completed, a bootcamp credential, even a polished LinkedIn profile, all of them tell a recruiter you sat through something and finished. Useful for learning, weak as a signal, because completion is not evidence of quality. They stop at the certificate. None of them put a judged piece of your actual work in front of the person deciding whether to talk to you. That gap, between finishing something and proving you are good at it, is exactly where no-experience candidates get stuck. The one signal that flips the read Give the recruiter something to evaluate. The reason proxies dominate is not that anyone loves them, it is that nothing better is usually in the file. Drop in a real, scored piece of work and the math changes completely. A recruiter can open a marketing brief, a product spec, or a data analysis that has already been graded against a professional standard, and form a genuine judgment in roughly the same seconds they would have spent skimming bullets, except now they are reacting to the work instead of guessing from a claim about it. Being evaluated instead of inferred is the whole game for someone with no experience, because evaluation is where good work beats a thin resume. And the market is already walking toward you. Skills-based hiring climbed to 85% of employers in 2025, up from 81% the year before , while reliance on the resume keeps slipping. More recruiters than ever are actively hunting for demonstrated ability over pedigree. Leading with proof is not swimming against the current. It hands them the exact thing they are increasingly trying to find, and that they almost never get from a first-time candidate. How a student builds that proof from scratch Produce one real thing and get it judged honestly. Pick the role you would take an entry-level job in today, marketing, product, data, design, then do an actual task from that role on one narrow problem. Not a course module, the work itself: a positioning brief, a spec with trade-offs and a metric, an analysis that ends in a recommendation. Then have it scored against the bar a strong professional would be held to, so its quality is established, not asserted by you. That scoring step is what makes the work credible to a recruiter, and it is also what makes you better. A score from someone qualified to give it turns your work from something you made into something that has been vetted, which is precisely the assurance an empty file is missing. zero is built to produce exactly that: you do company-shaped tasks, your work gets scored against a professional bar, and the scored result becomes proof a recruiter can open and judge before they ever ask for a transcript. It is free for students, because the recruiters pay for access to the people whose work already cleared the bar. FAQ What do recruiters look for in a candidate with no experience? A fast, credible signal that you can actually do the work. With no work history to read, recruiters fall back on proxies like school name and keywords, none of which prove anything. What earns real attention is evidence: a scored piece of work in the role they can open and judge for themselves, instead of guessing from a list of claims. How long do recruiters spend on a resume? Seconds, on the first pass, and often a piece of software screens you before a human sees anything. That is why one more dense bullet list rarely moves the outcome for a no-experience candidate. One strong, evaluable work sample does more in those seconds than another paragraph about how motivated you are. Do recruiters care about GPA or school name? Less than they used to, and far less than students fear. Skills-based hiring hit 85% of employers in 2025, up from 81%, so demonstrated ability keeps outranking pedigree. GPA and school still break ties in a few places, but the signal trending up is evidence you can do the work. How do you stand out with no experience? Give recruiters something to evaluate instead of something to take on faith. Build a real work sample in your target role, get it scored against a professional bar, and put it where recruiters can see it. Judged work separates you from a stack of identical resumes faster than anything you can write about yourself. Related reads How do you prove you can do the job before you have the job? ## what happens when you graduate into a recession and how do you get hired anyway
URL: https://learn.zero.university/learn/what-happens-when-you-graduate-into-a-recession
Home / Learn / what happens when you graduate into a recession and how do you get hired anyway CORNERSTONE what happens when you graduate into a recession and how do you get hired anyway You enter a market where entry-level roles shrink first, competition triples, and credential inflation spikes, and the students who get hired anyway are the ones who can prove they can ship work on day one, not the ones who waited four years for a signal that no longer guarantees an interview. New-grad hiring at big tech is down more than 50% from 2019, with new grads now representing only ~7% of hires, SignalFire State of Talent Report 2025 An internship cuts your odds of underemployment by 48.5%, but formal programs vanish first in downturns, Strada Institute + Burning Glass Institute, "Talent Disrupted" (Feb 2024) Resume use among employers fell to 67% in 2025, down from 73% the year before, as hiring managers seek faster ways to verify capability, TestGorilla State of Skills-Based Hiring 2025 When two candidates look equal on paper, employers rank "an internship with their organization or within their industry" as the most influential differentiator, NACE The recession-proof move: build verifiable work samples in the exact format hiring managers use to evaluate candidates, so you bypass the resume pile entirely. why do entry-level jobs disappear first in a recession? Companies do not stop hiring in recessions. They stop gambling. When budgets tighten, the first cuts hit roles with the longest payoff curves. Entry-level positions require months of training before the employee generates value. In a contraction, that timeline looks like luxury spending. Senior hires who can execute immediately become the priority. Internship programs shrink or convert to return-offer pipelines only. The result: a class of graduates competing for fewer structured on-ramps, while experienced workers displaced from higher levels trickle down into mid-level roles that used to absorb new talent. This is why the "just get any job to start" advice from 2010-era recovery breaks down. The 2008 recession created a lost generation of graduates who never caught up to peers who entered in stronger years. The gap persists in lifetime earnings data. Recession graduation is not a temporary inconvenience. It is a structural disadvantage that compounds unless you actively counter it. The counter is not another credential. In 2008, more graduates fled to law school and MBA programs, emerging two or three years later into markets that had not improved and now featured more degree holders competing for the same shrunken pool. The degree-as-escape-hatch strategy assumes the credential itself carries hiring power independent of market conditions, but when hiring managers face pressure to make every hire count, they ignore the signal and look for evidence. what actually changes in how employers evaluate candidates? Recession hiring accelerates a shift that was already underway: the move from proxy signals to verified capability. In boom times, a prestigious degree plus a decent GPA could open doors because the cost of a bad hire felt absorbable. In a downturn, every mis-hire threatens headcount that took political capital to protect. Hiring managers get explicit or implicit pressure to justify selections with something stronger than "they went to a good school." The resume, already declining in relevance, becomes a liability when it is the only artifact a candidate offers. Resume use among employers dropped to 67% in 2025, continuing a slide that recessions steepen rather than reverse. What replaces it? Work samples, scored assessments, and direct evidence of having done the job already. The 85% of employers now using skills-based hiring are not doing it because it is fashionable. They are doing it because it reduces time-to-productivity and improves retention in roles where they cannot afford turnover. In a recession, this preference hardens into requirement. The practical implication for a 2026 or 2027 graduate: your competition is not just the classmate with the better GPA, but also the bootcamp graduate with three deployed projects, the career switcher with a portfolio of freelance work, the self-taught candidate who built something real and can walk through the decisions. They do not need the hiring manager to trust a credential because they bring the interview with them. how do you build proof when no one will give you a chance? The trap is waiting for permission. The escape is simulating the work without the job title. Internships exist because they reduce uncertainty for employers. A candidate who has already operated in a similar environment, with similar tools, toward similar outcomes, is de-risked. But internship programs are the first to freeze in downturns, and the ones that remain often require prior experience you do not have. The solution is to create the same de-risking effect through independent work that mirrors professional output. This means more than "build a project." It means building in the format that hiring managers actually evaluate: a scoped task with constraints, a decision record, a deliverable that could ship. A marketing student who runs actual paid ads for a friend's business and documents the CPM, CTR, and iteration logic brings more to an interview than one who completed a case study with no real budget at risk. A software candidate who debugs production-like code under time pressure, explains the trade-offs, and ships a working feature demonstrates what a leetcode grind cannot. The key is evidence density per minute of review. A hiring manager spending 30 seconds on your materials needs to see capability, not potential. Recession hiring compresses timelines. The candidate who makes the reviewer feel confident in under a minute gets the interview, while the one who requires a leap of faith does not. what should you do differently if you graduate into a downturn? Three shifts matter, and they all involve abandoning the default path that worked for your parents' generation. First, compress the feedback loop. The old model: spend four years accumulating credentials, then shop them to employers who may or may not value them. The recession model: generate work, get it evaluated against a professional bar, iterate, and repeat on a weekly cycle. Each cycle produces an artifact that can be shown. After ten cycles you have a portfolio that no single internship could have built, because internships often assign grunt work that never sees evaluation. Second, target the hiring manager's actual fear. In a recession the fear is not "will this person be adequate?" but rather "will this person be productive in week two and still here in month six?" Your materials should answer both. Show work that required judgment, not just execution. Show iteration based on feedback, not just finished products. Show that you have already failed and adjusted, because recessions produce failures and employers need people who do not freeze. Third, abandon the application lottery. Mass-applying through job boards in a recession is a low-return activity because the ratio of applicants to roles balloons. The effective strategy is narrow targeting: identify companies that are actually hiring (not just posting), understand their specific constraints, and approach with a customized work sample that demonstrates you have already thought about their problem. This requires more research per application and yields fewer applications total, and in a flooded market, specificity is the only attention mechanism that works. is a recession actually the worst time to graduate? It is the worst time to graduate with only a degree, and it can be the best time to graduate with proof. Recessions force clarity. The candidates who relied on credential inflation, networking alone, or the assumption that demand would meet supply are exposed. The candidates who built verifiable capability find that the noise reduction works in their favor. When every hiring manager is skeptical, the one candidate who removes skepticism wins disproportionately. The data on this is longitudinal, not immediate. The graduates of 2008 and 2009 who entered the workforce without direction or evidence took years to recover. The ones who used the downturn to build skills that the recovery would need, data analysis, digital operations, direct response marketing, automation, emerged with trajectories that exceeded the pre-recession baseline. The recession itself did not determine outcomes. The response to it did. The structural replacement for the degree was always coming, and a recession does not create the replacement: it just removes the temporary conditions that made the old system look functional. frequently asked questions Should I go to grad school if I graduate into a recession? Only if the degree directly unlocks a credential-gated role you are certain you want. Using grad school as a waiting room assumes the market will improve and the additional credential will matter. Both assumptions failed for many 2008-2010 graduates who emerged with more debt into markets that had not recovered. Build proof instead. Do companies still hire new grads in a recession? Yes, but selectively and in smaller numbers. New-grad hiring at big tech is down more than 50% from 2019. The roles that remain go to candidates who can demonstrate immediate productivity. The hiring does not stop, but the margin for error does. How do I get experience if no one will hire me without experience? By creating work that does not require permission. Run real campaigns, build real tools, analyze real datasets, document real decisions. The experience employers value is not the job title but having operated under constraints and produced output. Simulate those conditions independently, get your work scored against professional standards, and present the evidence. Is networking more important than skills in a recession? Networking gets you the conversation, and skills get you the offer. In a recession, hiring managers face personal risk for bad hires, so referrals matter less unless the referee can also vouch for capability. The most effective network is one where your work preceded you and the contact can describe what you built, not just who you are. What industries hire during recessions? Some sectors are counter-cyclical: healthcare, utilities, debt collection, certain government functions, and businesses that help other businesses cut costs. But the better question is which roles within any industry become essential. Operations, revenue operations, customer retention, and automation tend to persist because they directly affect survival. Target functions, not just sectors. Keep reading How to get a job with no experience (the method that actually works) How do you prove you can do the job before you have the job? ## what do hiring managers actually discuss in debriefs about junior candidates
URL: https://learn.zero.university/learn/what-hiring-managers-say-in-debriefs-junior-candidates
Home / Learn / what do hiring managers actually discuss in debriefs about junior candidates CORNERSTONE what do hiring managers actually discuss in debriefs about junior candidates They do not debate your GPA, they argue whether you can actually do the work, whether you will quit in six months, and whether anyone on the team wants to manage you. The debrief is a risk-assessment session disguised as a meeting. Only 53% of employers have dropped degree requirements , but most still screen on pedigree because it feels safer than judging skill. New-grad hiring at big tech is down more than 50% from 2019 , so every junior slot carries more scrutiny and higher stakes. Internship-to-full-time conversion is 63.1% , which means managers already know what "proven" looks like and compare every external candidate against that bar. Hiring managers spend the bulk of debrief time on two questions: "will they ship" and "will they stay," not "did they interview well." do they even look at my coursework? Almost never. A hiring manager at a Series B fintech put it bluntly in a debrief we observed: "I do not care that she took machine learning at Stanford. I care that she cannot explain why she picked random forest over logistic regression on a real dataset." Coursework is shorthand for exposure, not proof. In the debrief, it gets mentioned only as a tiebreaker between two candidates who both showed they can execute, or as a red flag when someone leans on a brand-name course instead of showing the work. The real signal they hunt for is evidence of completion under constraint. Did you build something that had users, deadlines, or stakeholders? A GitHub repo with three commits and no README reads as "started and abandoned." A project where you describe why you killed a feature reads as "someone who ships, learns, and moves on." Managers know that university projects are usually sandboxed: no real users, no real failure, no real maintenance. They are not hostile to them. They are just not moved by them. This is why the shift to skills-based hiring is messier than the headline suggests. Many managers who dropped degree requirements still default to signals they trust: internships, referrals, brand-name programs. The debrief exposes the gap between policy and practice. Someone says "skills-based," then asks "but where did they intern?" The contradiction is not hypocrisy. It is uncertainty. Managers need a way to calibrate risk, and without scored proof of work, they retreat to the old proxies. what is the "airport test" and does it actually matter? Yes, and it is more honest than most hiring rhetoric. The airport test is simple: would I want to be stuck at an airport with this person during a six-hour delay? In debriefs, it surfaces as "team fit," "culture add," or "vibe check." For junior candidates, it carries outsized weight because the manager knows they will spend more time teaching you than delegating to you. If the teaching feels like dentistry, you are out. The catch is that "fit" is often evaluated in the narrow window of a 45-minute interview, where extroverts perform and introverts recede. Debriefs sometimes catch this bias, sometimes reinforce it. A manager who loved your energy may frame it as "curiosity" while a quieter candidate's identical preparation gets labeled "rote." The best debriefs name this explicitly. The worst ones do not even realize it happened. For you, the implication is tactical: show that you can collaborate without performing collaboration. Ask a specific question about the team's current bottleneck. Reference something the interviewer said earlier and build on it. In debriefs, these moments get reported as "listened" and "engaged," which are rarer than you would expect. Most junior candidates treat interviews as oral exams. The ones who advance treat them as working sessions. how do they compare me to the internal intern who already knows the codebase? This is the silent killer in most junior debriefs. There is almost always an internal candidate, a former intern, or a referral who already has context. You are not being evaluated in a vacuum. You are being weighed against someone who proved they can function in this specific environment. The 63.1% internship conversion rate exists because companies already made that bet and won. In debriefs, this comparison is explicit: "Rachel already knows our stack and shipped a feature in August." The external candidate then needs to show something that offsets that advantage. Usually, it is speed of learning or quality of work product. But "I learn fast" is unverifiable in an interview. What shifts the conversation is evidence: a project where you entered an unfamiliar codebase and contributed within a week, a writeup of how you diagnosed a bug in a technology you had never used. The degree-as-mortgage analogy fits here: you borrowed time and money for an asset that does not automatically clear the bar against someone who already has equity in the firm, and the intern has equity while you need proof of return. Not a transcript. Not a certificate. Proof that you can generate value before you have been taught the full playbook. what makes a manager fight for me versus stay quiet? Advocacy in debriefs is not about being the best candidate. It is about being the easiest candidate to defend if you fail. A manager who champions you is making a reputation bet. They need a story they can tell their own manager if you do not work out: "She showed me X in the interview, and that is exactly what we needed." If your interview left no specific artifact, there is nothing to champion. The specific artifact can be surprisingly small. One hiring manager described fighting for a junior designer because "she walked me through why she rejected her own first iteration, and her reasoning was better than most senior designers I have worked with." Another passed on a candidate with a perfect GPA because "every answer started with 'in my class we learned,' and I could not picture her without a syllabus." What both examples share is evidence of independent judgment. Not correctness. Judgment. The debrief is where interviewers test whether their positive read was real or just charisma. They replay your answers and ask: "would they have done that if no one was grading it?" This is why scored, submitted work changes the dynamic entirely, because it is evidence of judgment under real conditions, not interview conditions, and a manager can point to your submission and say, "this is what they produced when no one was watching." why do some debriefs end with "let's keep looking" even when I was good? Because good is not the standard. The standard is "clearly better than the cost of onboarding and the risk of early departure." With new-grad hiring compressed , every junior hire is a portfolio decision. Managers know that training you will consume senior hours that could go to shipping. They need conviction that the investment pays back. "Keep looking" often means no one in the room could answer the basic question: what would this person actually do in week three? If the role is vague and your profile is general, the debrief stalls. If you have a specific project or skill that maps to a specific team need, someone can argue for you. Otherwise, you become a "maybe for another role" that never materializes. The honest frame is that most companies do not have a structured junior path. They have senior problems and hope juniors can grow into solving them. The debrief exposes whether that hope feels grounded or desperate. Your job in the interview is to make it feel grounded by showing you have already done something adjacent to their reality, not something adjacent to a classroom. faq do hiring managers ever look at my linkedin recommendations? Rarely in debriefs. They are seen as too generic to risk-calibrate. A specific note from a former manager about how you handled a crisis gets mentioned. "Great to work with" does not. does asking questions at the end actually change the debrief? Yes, if the questions are specific to the team's work. Generic questions about culture or growth get forgotten. A question like "how did you decide to build in-house versus buy for X" gets quoted as "actually thinks about tradeoffs." should i mention my side projects if they are not polished? Polished is not the bar. Finished and explained is. A rough project where you can articulate what you learned, what you cut, and why you moved on beats a perfect tutorial clone you cannot modify. how do debriefs differ at startups versus large companies? Startups optimize for "can they run with ambiguity." Large companies optimize for "will they survive our process." The startup debrief asks if you will quit when there is no manager. The corporate debrief asks if you will quit when there is too many. is there a "junior premium" where they expect me to be cheaper? Not really. They expect you to be net-negative for months, then hopefully break even. The cost is time, not salary. Debriefs focus on whether you will survive long enough to become productive, not whether you will negotiate hard. How to build a portfolio without work experience A portfolio beats a résumé only when the work inside it has been scored against a professional bar. By the zero team. Last updated: 2026-06-08


## What is a job simulation, and is it worth it?
URL: https://learn.zero.university/learn/what-is-a-job-simulation-and-is-it-worth-it
Home / Learn / What is a job simulation, and is it worth it? CORNERSTONE What is a job simulation, and is it worth it? A job simulation hands you a real task from a real role and has you produce the actual deliverable, then evaluates what you made. It is the closest thing to doing the job before you have it. Whether it is worth your time hangs on one question: does anyone who hires ever see the result? A job simulation makes you produce the real work of a role instead of answering questions about it, which is exactly the evidence employers are shifting toward: 85% of employers now use skills-based hiring methods , and resume use fell to 67%. Real work experience is the strongest protective factor in the data: a single internship cuts the odds of underemployment by 48.5%, per Strada and the Burning Glass Institute . Simulations exist to give you that kind of evidence without waiting for someone to hire you first. Most simulations end in a certificate nobody opens, so their hiring value stays low even when the learning is real. The version worth your time leaves you with scored work a recruiter can actually evaluate. Employers talk a better skills game than they play: fewer than 1 in 700 hires reflected real change after companies dropped degree requirements . Your job is to make your proof impossible to ignore, not to trust the trend. What exactly is a job simulation? A job simulation drops you into the work of one specific role and asks you to produce what someone in that seat actually produces. Not a quiz about the work, the work itself. You get a scenario shaped like a company problem, the context and constraints a professional would have, and a deliverable to make. Then your output gets evaluated, anywhere from a quick automated check to a scored review against a professional standard, depending on the platform. The defining trait is the artifact. At the end you have made the same kind of thing a working professional hands their manager. That single difference separates simulations from nearly everything else students reach for: courses teach you concepts and check that you remember them, assessment tests score recall under a clock, and a simulation skips to the part hiring actually cares about, which is whether you can do the work at all. What does a job simulation look like in practice? Five concrete examples, one per role, of what you would actually produce: Role Simulated task What you walk away with Marketing Position a product for a launch the company cannot afford to fumble A positioning brief and campaign plan with real trade-offs Product Decide what ships next quarter with engineering capacity for one big bet A spec with prioritized trade-offs and a success metric Data Investigate why a key metric dropped 14% and recommend a response A short analysis that lands on a defensible recommendation Design Redesign a signup flow that loses half its users at step two A flow with annotated decisions, not just pretty screens Finance Build the case for or against entering a new market A model plus a one-page recommendation a CFO could act on Notice what every artifact has in common: judgment under constraints. That is the thing no transcript shows and the thing interviewers spend their whole hour trying to detect. A good simulation produces evidence of it on paper. What types of job simulations exist? The label covers four fairly different animals, and knowing which one you are looking at tells you most of what it is worth: Type What it is Who sees your work Course-attached projects A capstone bolted onto a video course Usually nobody; you get a completion certificate Employer hiring assessments Work-sample tests inside a specific company's hiring process That one employer, for that one opening Open practice simulations Free, self-paced company-branded tasks, the Forage model Mostly you; the certificate goes on your resume, the work rarely gets read Recruiting-connected simulations Real role tasks scored against a professional bar, with the scored work shown to recruiters, the zero model The people deciding whether to interview you The first three are not useless. Practice is practice, and a hiring assessment is a simulation you should absolutely take seriously because a job sits on the other side of it. But only the last type converts your effort into a standing asset that works for you across many employers at once. So is a job simulation worth it? Worth it for learning: almost always. Worth it for getting hired: only if the output travels. Here is the blunt test nobody selling simulations likes to answer: after you finish, does anyone who hires ever see the result? Most of the market fails that test. You spend six hours producing genuinely decent work, the platform hands you a PDF certificate, and the work itself goes into a folder nobody will ever open. The learning was real, but as a hiring signal you are holding a participation badge in a market that has stopped paying for badges, where 53% of employers have already dropped degree requirements for some roles and are looking for direct evidence of capability instead. One warning before you bet your season on the trend. Employers adopted the language of skills faster than the practice: the Burning Glass Institute found that after companies removed degree requirements, fewer than 1 in 700 hires actually reflected the change . The trend is real but slow, which means weak proof gets you nothing. The bar for evidence that changes a recruiter's mind is high: scored, specific, and visible. Do a simulation when: You have no internships yet and need your first real evidence of capability You are switching fields and your degree says nothing about the role you want You are deciding whether you would even like the day-to-day work of a role, before spending a summer on it The simulation ends with your work evaluated and visible to people who hire Skip it when: You are collecting certificates to decorate a resume; recruiters stopped reading those The platform cannot answer who sees your finished work You already have strong real-world proof and the simulation would just duplicate it How does a job simulation compare to an internship, a course, or a certificate? What it proves Who sees it Cost to you Internship You did the job, in the strongest form there is One employer deeply; others take it on faith from one resume line A competitive application season and a summer Job simulation You can do the work of the role Depends entirely on the type; from nobody to every recruiter on the platform Hours to days, usually free Course You studied the material Whoever reads the certificate line Weeks to months, often paid Certificate You finished something Recruiters see the line and rarely weight it Varies; the signal value is the problem, not the price The internship is still the gold standard, and the numbers say why: 63.1% of interns convert to full-time offers , and an internship is the single most influential factor when recruiters choose between two otherwise equal candidates. The honest case for simulations is not that they beat internships. It is that they are the fastest way to build internship-grade evidence when you do not have one, and the best preparation for converting the one you eventually get. We wrote up the direct comparison in virtual simulation vs real internship . Where can you actually do a job simulation? An honest map of the options: Forage offers free, self-paced simulations branded by real companies. Good for exploring what work in a field feels like and for showing initiative. The limit is structural: your work is not scored against a standard and recruiters do not review it, so it functions as practice plus a resume line. Our full breakdown: Forage alternatives for students . Employer assessments appear inside specific hiring processes. You do not choose these; they choose you. Treat every one as a simulation with a job attached. zero is built around recruiting-connected simulation: you take on company-shaped tasks in the role you are aiming for, your deliverable is scored against a professional bar, and the scored work is shown to recruiters. It is free for students because recruiters pay for access to the talent. Do-it-yourself is underrated: pick a real company, write the positioning brief or teardown they never asked for, and publish it. No score and no distribution, but real proof of initiative. We cover this play in how to prove you can do the job before you have it . Why does learning by doing beat memorize-and-test? Because of what each one leaves behind. Memorize-and-test leaves you with decaying recall and a grade that tells employers almost nothing, while producing real work leaves you with a skill you exercised plus an artifact that proves it, and the artifact keeps working for you long after the knowledge fades. Education research has said this for decades; the labor market is just now pricing it in. The school path optimizes for filtration, passing you through gate after gate without ever asking you to make anything, which is a big part of why new grads are down to roughly 7% of big-tech hires while employers complain they cannot find capable juniors. The capability gap is real and it is exactly the gap simulations exist to close. How do zero's simulations work? zero is built on simulation, but it starts from the goal the rest of the field keeps forgetting: getting your real work in front of the people who hire. You take on company-shaped tasks in the role you are aiming for. You produce the actual deliverable, not a quiz about it. Your work gets scored against the standard strong professionals are held to, with feedback specific enough to act on. Then that scored work is shown to recruiters, who can open it and judge it before they ever look at your transcript. Recruiters pay for access to that talent, which is why zero stays free for students. You learn and prove capability in the same motion, and that is the only kind of job simulation that actually moves you toward a job. FAQ Are job simulations free? Mostly yes. Forage simulations are free, employer assessments cost nothing but effort, and zero is free for students because recruiters fund the platform. Be skeptical of paid simulations: you are usually paying for a certificate, and certificates are the weakest part of the value. How long does a job simulation take? Anywhere from two hours to a few days of real work. That is the point: it compresses the evidence-building of an internship into a fraction of the time. If one promises mastery in twenty minutes, it is a quiz wearing a costume. Can I put a job simulation on my resume? Yes, and you should, but list the work, not the badge. "Built a campaign plan for a product launch, scored 87 against a professional rubric" reads completely differently from "Completed virtual experience program." If the simulation gave you a scored artifact, link it. Do employers actually care about job simulations? They care about evidence of capability, and a simulation is only as strong as the evidence it produces. A certificate alone moves little. Scored work they can open and judge is a different conversation, especially with 85% of employers now using skills-based hiring methods. Can a job simulation replace an internship? Not fully, and be suspicious of anyone who says otherwise. An internship remains the strongest single signal. What a simulation does is get you internship-grade evidence faster, make you a stronger internship applicant, and cover you if the internship never materializes. Full answer: can simulations replace internships on a resume . Are Forage certificates worth anything? As learning and field-exploration, yes. As a differentiator, less than you hope: they are free and unscored, so completing one signals interest more than capability. Pair one with real scored work and you get the best of both. Which roles can you simulate? Marketing, product, data, design, finance, consulting, software, and operations all simulate well, because each produces a reviewable artifact. If a role's core output can be put in front of an expert and judged, it can be simulated. What is the catch with free simulations? The business model tells you. Free-and-unscored usually means the platform is selling courses or brand exposure, and your work is exhaust. Free-because-recruiters-pay means your work is the product, which is exactly what you want it to be. Related reads How does a virtual job simulation compare to a real internship?
